{"id": "12:26/q16", "question": "What does 'he is among the liars' specify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q16/p1", "position": "It would make Joseph false in his claim that she solicited him.", "reasons": "Alusi says lying concerns Joseph's specific counterclaim; he adds that truth and falsehood can apply to explicit statements and their implications."}]}
{"id": "12:26/q17", "question": "Does the shirt test support legal judgment from circumstantial signs?", "turns_on": "Whether the witness was an adult drawing a fallible inference or an infant whose miraculous speech was conclusive.", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q17/p1", "position": "Yes, an adult witness's reasoned use of the tear supports judging from indicators.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya cites jurists who use the verse; Qurtubi makes the legal inference conditional on an adult witness. He cites Malik on disputed goods held by thieves and Muhammad, Shurayh, and Iyas on allocating household property by its apparent use."}, {"id": "12:26/q17/p2", "position": "If the witness was a speaking infant, his miracle proves the case without establishing that legal inference.", "reasons": "Qurtubi distinguishes miraculous infant testimony from an adult's deduction; Nahhas and Jubba'i likewise say an infant's speech itself is stronger proof than the shirt."}]}
{"id": "12:26/q18", "question": "How does this shirt connect to Joseph's other shirts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q18/p1", "position": "Joseph's shirt serves as evidence at three narrative stages.", "reasons": "Mawardi names the false blood exposing the brothers in 12:18, the rear tear vindicating Joseph, and the shirt restoring Jacob's sight in 12:96. Sha'bi adds that a wolf would have torn the bloodied shirt and cites 12:93. Samarrai connects the shirt to slavery, prison and reunion."}]}
{"id": "12:26/q19", "question": "How many cradle-speakers include Joseph's witness, and how are the reports assessed?", "turns_on": "The competing transmitted lists and whether the Sahihayn's three-speaker report is exhaustive.", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q19/p1", "position": "A four-speaker report includes Joseph's witness, Jesus, Jurayj's companion, and Pharaoh's hairdresser's child.", "reasons": "Reports attributed to Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra, and the Prophet give four, with variant wording and ordering. Alusi reports Suyuti's authentication through Ahmad, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim. Suyuti says al-Tibi sought reconciliation; a narrow-versus-broad infancy reconciliation is called strained by Alusi."}, {"id": "12:26/q19/p2", "position": "Some lists name three speakers and create tension with the four-speaker report.", "reasons": "Abu Hurayra names Jesus, Joseph's companion and Jurayj's companion; Hilal says the witness was one of three. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that Bukhari and Muslim list only three, including a nursing infant instead of Joseph's witness; al-Tibi objects on that basis."}, {"id": "12:26/q19/p3", "position": "An expanded account names five or as many as eleven cradle-speakers.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya mentions a report adding Pharaoh's hairdresser's son as fifth; Suyuti adds a nursing infant and a People of the Ditch child and gathers eleven in a poem, while noting Zamakhshari's fifth."}]}
{"id": "12:26/q20", "question": "How does the verse relate to the wider story and other scriptures?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q20/p1", "position": "The Qur'anic episode differs from Genesis and illustrates divine direction through events.", "reasons": "Asad says Genesis lacks 12:26–34 and has the husband believe the accusation immediately and imprison Joseph; the Qur'anic sura illustrates God's hidden direction, compared with 2:216."}, {"id": "12:26/q20/p2", "position": "The wife's later admission and Joseph's later authority illuminate the outcome.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata says she was not yet wholly absorbed in love, later preferred Joseph and confessed in 12:51. Burhan contrasts her desire and failed worldly power with Joseph's obedience and eventual authority in 12:56."}, {"id": "12:26/q20/p3", "position": "The passage's arrangement calls for contemplation as part of Qur'anic inimitability.", "reasons": "Burhan urges attention to its order and compares 40:28."}]}
{"id": "12:26/q21", "question": "What other nearby wording and linguistic examples do the sources note?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q21/p1", "position": "Related remarks concern adjacent accusations, cuts, and other cited readings.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says bisūʾin need mean only unpleasant conduct, even harsh address or striking. Samin also reports qut instead of qudd, Yaqub's distinction for intact skin or cloth, and a poetry example. Bint Shati compares unique qidada in 72:11 with the shirt's tearing. Nashr records assimilation examples from al-Kahf and 72:3 and a class of vowel patterns at other verses."}]}
{"id": "12:27/q01", "question": "How are the witness's conditional words attached to the report of testimony?", "turns_on": "Whether testimony must be recast as an omitted saying or can itself govern reported speech.", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q01/p1", "position": "An omitted verb of saying introduces the conditional, because the testimony is treated as speech.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari compares the ellipsis to the inheritance statement in 4:11. Al-Mazini posits omitted qawl. Al-Baydawi allows either quoted speech or testimony construed as speech; al-Nasafi supplies 'the witness said.' Al-Alusi attributes this analysis to Basran grammarians."}, {"id": "12:27/q01/p2", "position": "The conditionals are governed directly by shahida as reported speech.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports that Kufan grammarians allow shahida to govern the quoted conditions."}]}
{"id": "12:27/q02", "question": "How can past-tense كان follow the conditional إن?", "turns_on": "Whether the past form keeps past force, expresses future discovery, or has a broader verbal use.", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q02/p1", "position": "It means 'if it becomes known or turns out that the shirt was torn,' so the discovery lies ahead.", "reasons": "Abu Ishaq glosses it as in yuʿlam: knowledge has yet to occur, and cites Zuhayr's poetry for past form with this force; al-Nahhas also cites the line. Al-Baydawi compares a conditional that states past kindness after a future condition. Al-Nasafi says future-oriented in concerns what the inspection will reveal; al-Nahhas calls the construction conditional and jussive, noting that conditions normally project past verbs into the future."}, {"id": "12:27/q02/p2", "position": "Kāna retains its past-time meaning even in the conditional.", "reasons": "Al-Samin reports al-Mubarrad's view and contrasts it with another view that makes the verb future-oriented as other conditional verbs are; the clause serves clarification."}, {"id": "12:27/q02/p3", "position": "Kāna is broad enough to express all actions.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas reports Muhammad ibn Yazid's explanation without a narrower temporal gloss."}]}
{"id": "12:27/q03", "question": "Who is the witness who proposed the shirt test?", "turns_on": "Whether the proof came through an adult relative's inference, miraculous infant speech, or the shirt itself as witness.", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q03/p1", "position": "A wise or trusted adult from the woman's family proposed it; reports variously call him her cousin, a consulted man, or possibly a judge.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi locates the husband and her cousin at the door; Ibn Ishaq calls him a trusted man of Qitfir's family. Al-Nahhas prefers a wise adult consulted by the king, cites repeated reports from Ibn Abbas that he was not a child, and allows that an infant-speaking hadith could mean a young person rather than a small child. Al-Alusi's observing relative uses the sign to avoid shaming her; he doubts that direction alone could convince a wise judge. Kuran Yolu calls an experienced family member likely, reports Maududi's possible judge with uncertainty, and stresses his fairness despite kinship. Study Quran reports the wise paternal-cousin identification."}, {"id": "12:27/q03/p2", "position": "The witness was an infant whose speech itself vindicated Joseph.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas argues against a small child: such speech would be a clearer miracle than inference from the shirt, while the hadith of four infant speakers can be read as referring to a young person. Al-Alusi reports a critic's argument that infant speech alone would suffice even if the signs did not match, and prefers a rear-sign/front-foil explanation for the infant account."}, {"id": "12:27/q03/p3", "position": "The torn shirt itself served as the witness.", "reasons": "Mujahid identifies the rear-torn shirt as the witness; the report also speaks of a judge who says the shirt will clarify the affair. Qatada says the shirt itself adjudicated."}]}
{"id": "12:27/q04", "question": "How does this shirt connect with the other shirt signs in Joseph's story?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q04/p1", "position": "It is one of three shirt signs: its rear tear proves Joseph truthful, false blood exposes the wolf story, and it later restores Jacob's sight.", "reasons": "ʿAmir in Ibn Abi Hatim says a real wolf would also have torn the shirt (12:18) and cites its restoration of sight (12:93). Al-Mawardi likewise links false blood and the shirt placed on Jacob's face (12:96)."}]}
{"id": "12:27/q05", "question": "What does قُدَّ mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q05/p1", "position": "It means to tear.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shatiʾ says the root retains this basic sense in the unique Qur'anic form qidada and in Joseph's shirt torn from the front or back; she mentions 72:11, 12:25, and 12:28."}]}

{"id": "12:27/q07", "question": "How is the direction word دُبُرٍ read, with its paired قُبُل?", "turns_on": "Voweling, tanwīn, and whether the nouns remain inflected or are treated as fixed direction terms.", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q07/p1", "position": "The common reading inflects the direction nouns with tanwīn and a sounded middle consonant.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan call it the majority reading; al-Samin says the expressions mean from behind and from in front, of the shirt or Joseph. Al-Samin adds al-ʿAtaridi and al-Jarud and mentions transmissions with a quiescent middle letter; Abu Hayyan, Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, and al-Alusi report related variants. Al-Alusi attributes a fatḥa reading to Ibn Ishaq."}, {"id": "12:27/q07/p4", "position": "Some lighten the direction words by stilling their middle consonant while retaining tanwīn or a genitive ending.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report shortened forms; Abu Hayyan reports silent bāʾ; al-Samin names al-Hasan and a transmission of Abu ʿAmr, calling it a Hijaz and Asad dialect. {"id": "12:27/q08", "question": "How is the direction noun after مِن construed?", "turns_on": "Whether the direction word is an indefinite inflected noun, a built endpoint with an omitted possessor, or a proper direction name.", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q08/p1", "position": "It is an inflected, indefinite noun naming a direction, whether the shirt's or Joseph's.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafi and al-Zamakhshari gloss it as a side called back; al-Samin allows the shirt or Joseph as the point of reference. Abu Hayyan reports al-Zamakhshari's shirt-specific explanation. Abu Hatim objects to treating such declinable nouns as built adverbs."}, {"id": "12:27/q08/p2", "position": "In the built reading it functions like a terminal adverb after an omitted possessor.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni compares 'before and after' in 30:4; al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan report suppressed possessors. Al-Samin says the built form analogizes to qabl and baʿd when severed from annexation, although its underlying form is an inflected noun, and cites Abu Hatim's objection that the construction belongs only to adverbs."}, {"id": "12:27/q08/p3", "position": "With fatḥa it is treated as a feminine proper name for a direction or endpoint.", "reasons": "Abu Ishaq calls front and back endpoints and permits fatḥa. {"id": "12:27/q09", "question": "What do the two uses of مِن contribute?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q09/p1", "position": "The first marks the starting point of the tear; the second is partitive, placing Joseph among the truthful.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi explicitly distinguishes the min used with front or back from the min in 'among the truthful.'"}]}
{"id": "12:27/q10", "question": "How does the tear's direction distinguish the two accounts?", "turns_on": "Whether front and rear tears both discriminate the parties physically, or the front case only frames the known rear tear; and how exclusive the physical inference is.", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q10/p1", "position": "A rear tear fits Joseph fleeing while she pursued and pulled him; a front tear would fit Joseph approaching or chasing her while she resisted.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Tabrisi, Ibn Kathir, al-Alusi, and Study Quran infer flight and pursuit from the rear tear; Ibn Ishaq reasons that an approaching man meets a woman from the front. Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Wahidi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan's report from al-Zamakhshari, and al-Alusi's reports spell out the front alternative: she might push Joseph away, or he might trip or catch his shirt while hurrying after her. Al-Alusi adds that a quick encounter makes a rear pull the simplest motion, without Joseph turning back, and that if he tripped while escaping she would naturally cling to him. The wife could be found lying and Joseph truthful on this test."}, {"id": "12:27/q10/p2", "position": "The front-tear scenarios are not exclusive: they could also happen while she pursued Joseph.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Munir criticizes the proposed pushing or tripping scenarios and regards pulling as the more likely cause. Al-Alusi answers that the rapid encounter still makes a rear pull the easier explanation of flight."}, {"id": "12:27/q10/p3", "position": "The front condition is a counterfactual setup; the actual rear tear is the decisive sign.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi prefers this for the infant-witness account, so the two conditions need not have equally matching physical explanations. Ibn al-Kamal says the witness already knew the rear tear and criticizes al-Baydawi's reading; al-Alusi says mentioning a hypothetical front tear can underscore its nonoccurrence, comparing denial of a specific message despite speaking to its addressee."}]}
{"id": "12:27/q11", "question": "How much proof does the shirt sign provide?", "turns_on": "Whether the tear is sufficient evidence, a corroborating sign, or secondary to an infant's miraculous speech.", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q11/p1", "position": "The direction of the shirt tear adjudicates the dispute.", "reasons": "Qatada says the shirt itself decided; al-Wahidi describes a test between truthful and lying parties. Al-Tabari and others explain why a rear tear accords with Joseph's escape. Al-Alusi says a rapid encounter makes this the simpler explanation."}, {"id": "12:27/q11/p2", "position": "For a wise adult judge, direction alone would not establish certainty.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi doubts that this inference would satisfy a wise judge; Ibn al-Munir's objection is that the supposed front-tear causes could occur even if she pursued him."}, {"id": "12:27/q11/p3", "position": "The shirt corroborated earlier indications against the woman rather than serving as the sole basis.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports al-Razi's explanation that the earlier signs fell short of certainty, so the shirt was added."}, {"id": "12:27/q11/p4", "position": "If the witness was an infant, his miraculous declaration itself proved Joseph innocent regardless of the shirt signs.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports the later critic's argument; al-Nahhas similarly says infant testimony would be a clearer miracle than inference from the shirt."}]}
{"id": "12:27/q12", "question": "Why is the front-tear condition stated before the rear-tear condition?", "turns_on": "Whether the first condition is a fair-looking alternative or a deliberate foil to a fact already known.", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q12/p1", "position": "It appears impartial and gently grants her possible truth before the reverse condition exposes her lie.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan says the sequence lets her be truthful first and calls Joseph a liar only indirectly. Abu Hayyan says kinship explains giving her first chance, with explicit subjects in each independent clause. The later critic quoted by al-Alusi says the witness knew the rear tear but presented the nonexistent front tear first to appear impartial; the observing-relative account adds concern to avoid public shame."}, {"id": "12:27/q12/p2", "position": "The front condition is a known counterfactual foil that makes the actual rear tear stand out.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Kamal says the witness knew the rear tear and criticizes al-Baydawi; al-Alusi prefers the rear-sign/front-foil treatment for an infant witness and says a hypothetical front tear can emphasize that it did not occur."}]}
{"id": "12:27/q13", "question": "Why are the truth and lie clauses stated explicitly?", "turns_on": "Whether the note explains the clauses' emphatic function or their implied temporal particle.", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q13/p1", "position": "They reinforce conclusions already implied by the shirt condition and make each party's status clear.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says the clauses reinforce the inference and explicitly name the subjects because each is independent. Abu Hayyan compares their parallelism with the obedience and disobedience saying."}, {"id": "12:27/q13/p2", "position": "The past verdict implies qad, bringing the past action near the present state.", "reasons": "Al-Samin says fakadhabat and the paired 'spoke truth' clause imply qad; a frozen verb needs no expressed or understood qad."}]}

{"id": "12:27/q17", "question": "What happened around the doorway before the shirt was examined?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q17/p1", "position": "She tried to accuse Joseph, he answered that she pursued him, and a family witness proposed examining the torn shirt.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi says the husband sat at the door with her cousin. {"id": "12:27/q18", "question": "What larger lesson is drawn from this episode?", "turns_on": "The sources draw different broad lessons from the narrative outcome.", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q18/p1", "position": "Obedience brings true happiness despite immediate hardship; pursuit of desire fails despite worldly power.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan contrasts the wife's failed desire with Joseph's obedience, which saved him from prison and led to authority; he mentions 12:56."}, {"id": "12:27/q18/p2", "position": "God directs human affairs beyond what people can foresee; what they dislike may be good and what they love harmful.", "reasons": "Asad treats the Qur'anic Joseph story as illustrating this principle and cites 2:216."}]}
{"id": "12:27/q19", "question": "What is significant about the arrangement of these verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:27/q19/p1", "position": "Their arrangement invites contemplation as part of the Qur'an's inimitability.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan urges attention to the ordering and mentions 40:28."}]}

{"id": "12:32/q01", "question": "What does 'that is the one' identify?", "turns_on": "Whether the demonstrative indicates Joseph or love.", "positions": [{"id": "12:32/q01/p1", "position": "Joseph, whose beauty explains her passion.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī and others identify Yusuf. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says pointing to what they see is strongest proof."}, {"id": "12:32/q01/p2", "position": "Her love for Joseph is the referent.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya offers love as the referent of both dhālika and fīhi; al-Qurṭubī and al-Samīn report it. {"id": "12:32/q02", "question": "Why the distant demonstrative and plural address?", "turns_on": "Whether distance signals distinction or separation.", "positions": [{"id": "12:32/q02/p1", "position": "It elevates Joseph's rare beauty and identifies the previously unknown slave.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī see exaltation; al-Ālūsī also notes his absence when first blamed. {"id": "12:32/q03", "question": "What does the opening fāʾ do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:32/q03/p1", "position": "It introduces the explanation of their amazement.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī calls it explanatory; Ibn ʿĀshūr paraphrases: if he is the angel you claim, this is the man you blamed me over."}]}
{"id": "12:32/q04", "question": "What were the women blaming her for?", "turns_on": "Whether blame concerns emotion or deliberate action.", "positions": [{"id": "12:32/q04/p1", "position": "Her love and infatuation with Joseph.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās explicitly says love.
